# Iowa penalty for animal rights activists who record protests upheld at Eighth Circuit
Iowa Citizens for Community Improvement and other animal rights advocates sued the state in 2017 claiming a state law aimed at protecting livestock facilities violates the First Amendment by imposing enhanced criminal penalties for using an electronic surveillance device to record or transmit images while trespassing.
ICCI appealed to the Eighth Circuit, arguing in a brief that Iowa’s statute — in contrast to ordinary trespass law — imposes “significantly enhanced” criminal sanctions “against ICCI’s staff and members who engage in the civil disobedience, if they also record the protests.”
Courts generally agree that freedom of speech includes expression through making and sharing videos, but the U.S. Supreme Court “has never held that a trespasser … may exercise general rights of free speech on property privately owned and used nondiscriminatorily for private purposes …,” Grasz wrote, quoting a high court decision from 1972.

Thus, he said, “We need not resolve this question because even assuming recording while trespassing implicates the First Amendment, ICCI’s as-applied challenge fails.”
A spokesperson for ICCI said Thursday’s ruling restricts the rights of “people who want to tell the truth about industrial food systems.”
“Big Ag and Farm Bureau want to hide the real story of factory farm livestock production from consumers,” Brenda Brink, an ICCI member from rural Story County, said in a statement Thursday. “But we will never give up, and we won’t let this ruling stop us from telling the truth about corporate ag. We will continue to fight for a just and sustainable food system, our family farmers and our communities.”

Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird insisted farmers and businesses should be able to operate without fear of trespassers.

# Eighth Circuit Rules Against Temporary Block of Iowa’s Book Ban and “Don’t-Say-LGBTQ” Law
The Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals today ruled against the preliminary injunction that had temporarily blocked key provisions of Iowa’s SF 496, a multi-part law that bans books with sexual content from K–12 school libraries and prohibits mention of LGBTQ+ identities in K–6 classrooms. It also forces school staff to out transgender students to their parents regardless of the safety risks involved.

# Case Explained: People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals, Inc. Iowa Citizens for Community Improvement v. Kimberly Reynolds

Court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit Filed: 2026-04-23 The Eighth Circuit affirmed the dismissal of ICCI's as-applied First Amendment challenge, holding that Iowa Code § 727.8A does not violate the Constitution when applied to prohibit recording on property after an owner requests removal but fails to explicitly demand cessation of filming. Applying strict scrutiny, the court reasoned that the statute is narrowly tailored to serve the compelling state interest in protecting private property rights and remains content-neutral regarding protected speech. Consequently, the district court's judgment stands, leaving the aggravated trespass provision enforceable against such recording activities without further judicial intervention.

jina.snippet:
Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds said the suite of criminal justice measures she signed into law Tuesday would help keep Iowa communities safer, and could prevent future crimes in instances like the death of Ashley Marie Hall.

Hall was killed in a shooting incident in April in Des Moines. Sharneeka Evans was [charged with first-degree murder](https://www.kcci.com/article/police-investigate-deadly-shooting-on-des-moines-north-side/70982218) in relation to Hall’s death. The shooting gained Republican lawmakers attention as reporting found Evans had an outstanding arrest warrant that was resolved just a week before the shooting at a [free warrant resolution clinic.](https://www.polkcountyiowa.gov/county-attorney/news/free-clinic-will-allow-residents-to-resolve-low-level-warrants/) The clinic washosted by Polk County Attorney’s Office, alongside the Polk County Criminal Justice Coordinating Council and other organizations April 3. The event allowed people with certain arrest warrants to resolve or reschedule their court cases and sign up for payment plans.

While the arrest warrants resolved at the clinic for Evans and other participants were for nonviolent, non-felony charges, GOP lawmakers linked Hall’s death to the event. Lawmakers passed [House File 2787](https://www.legis.iowa.gov/legislation/BillBook?ga=91&ba=HF2787), which prohibits public entities from hosting, sponsoring or providing funding for warrant resolution clinics in the future, creating a simple misdemeanor charge for public employees and officials who violate the ban, and stopping counties from accessing court debt funds if they hold such events.

Warrant resolution clinics are defined in the measure as a “prearranged, formal or informal, advertised event designed to allow individuals with outstanding arrest warrants to appear and resolve such warrants without being subject to immediate arrest and custodial processing.”

Five animal-welfare groups sued several Iowa officials, alleging Iowa Code § 727.8A violates their members’ First Amendment rights on its face and as applied. But we reversed and remanded because § 727.8A may be applied in at least some instances without violating the Constitution. See Animal Legal Def. Fund v. Reynolds, 89 F.4th 1071, 1082 (8th Cir. 2024). On remand, two groups pursued as-applied challenges, arguing the statute violates their members’ First Amendment rights when applied to prevent them from recording on property that is otherwise open to the public when the owner asks them to leave but does not ask them to stop recording. The district court1 dismissed these challenges, and one group, Iowa Citizens for Community Improvement (ICCI), appeals. Applying § 727.8A to proscribe ICCI’s members’ alleged conduct does not violate the First Amendment, so we affirm.

Conclusion For these reasons, we affirm the district court’s judgment dismissing ICCI’s as-applied challenge.

ICCI alleges its members are willing to suffer the consequences for ordinary trespass but the heightened penalties for trespass-surveillance have chilled their speech. ... Id. ICCI posts this content on its website and social media “to communicate the message of the protests to ICCI's members and the public, and thereby encourage people to join the work.”  ... In sum, we conclude the officials can apply § 727.8A to proscribe the conduct ICCI contends its members engage in. Its members’ recordings implicate Iowa's important state interest in protecting owner's property and privacy rights, these interests would be served less effectively without the statute, and the statute does not proscribe substantially more speech than necessary to achieve Iowa's legitimate ends.
